# Curriculum

The reading list for *Energy Economics of the Green Transition*.
It is regenerated from the course sources, so it always matches what the
lectures actually cite.

## Getting hold of the papers

The lecture notes are in this repository, as PDFs under `notes/`.

The papers are not. Most are published articles that I have no right to
redistribute openly, so they are not on Absalon either: read them through
the [Royal Danish Library](https://kb.dk/en) with your KU login. Go in
through the library rather than the publisher's front page, or you will hit
a paywall the university has already paid. Where an author's own open
version exists, it is linked below and you can read that instead.

**What is examinable.** Each lecture below lists what is *required*: the
sections of the lecture notes it builds on, and the one or two papers the
lecture works through. That, and only that, can be asked at the exam.
Everything listed as *supplementary* is there for those who want to go
further; it is never assumed.

Read the required material before the lecture. The lectures are workshops
on the papers, not summaries of them, and they assume you have read the
note sections they build on.


## 01. Introduction

**Background**

- **Berg (2026).** “A Simple Model of Abatement Costs.”  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/abatement-costs.pdf)
  
  *Eleven pages, and the place to start. Its section 2 framework comes back in the exercise classes.*
- **Berg (2026).** “Generation Technologies.”  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/technologies.pdf)
  
  *A catalogue rather than an argument: what each generating technology is, what it costs, and what a levelised cost does and does not say. Read it once, then use it as a lookup; Appendix C is a glossary written for exactly that.*


## 02. Energy markets and market design (guest lecture)

**Required**

- **Mulder (2023).** “Regulation of Energy Markets: Economic Mechanisms and Policy Evaluation.” Springer. Read section 3.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-16571-9)
  
  *The reading for the guest lecture.*


## 03. Dispatch and variable generation

**Required**

- **Berg (2026).** “Energy System Models.” Read sections 2 and 3, and appendix A if the duality argument is new to you.  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/energy-system-models.pdf)
  
  *The dispatch model, the price as a shadow value, a carbon tax and a cap; then the model repeated over a year of Danish wind and solar, and what that does to prices and to the value of each technology.*
- **Hirth (2013).** “The Market Value of Variable Renewables: The Effect of Solar Wind Power Variability on Their Relative Price.” *Energy Economics* 38, 218–236.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2013.02.004) · [Open version](https://neon.energy/Hirth-2013-Market-Value-Renewables-Solar-Wind-Power-Variability-Price.pdf)
  
  *The paper the lecture works through. The market value of wind and solar falls as their share rises, and the paper measures by how much. Section 3 of the note defines the same value factor in the same model.*

**Supplementary**

- **Joskow (2011).** “Comparing the Costs of Intermittent and Dispatchable Electricity Generating Technologies.” *American Economic Review: Papers & Proceedings* 101(3), 238–241.
  
  *Four pages on why comparing technologies by levelised cost is the wrong comparison. The argument the lecture starts from.*
- **López Prol, Steininger and Zilberman (2020).** “The Cannibalization Effect of Wind and Solar in the California Wholesale Electricity Market.” *Energy Economics* 85, 104552.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2019.104552)
  
  *Cannibalisation measured in Californian market data rather than in a model.*
- **Borenstein (2012).** “The Private and Public Economics of Renewable Electricity Generation.” *Journal of Economic Perspectives* 26(1), 67–92.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.26.1.67)
  
  *A survey, written for economists, of what renewable generation is worth privately and socially.*
- **Reichenberg, Ekholm and Boomsma (2023).** “Revenue and Risk of Variable Renewable Electricity Investment: The Cannibalization Effect under High Market Penetration.” *Energy* 284, 128419.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2023.128419) · [Open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06287)
  
  *What falling market value does to the revenue and the risk of investing in wind and solar.*
- **Heptonstall and Gross (2021).** “A Systematic Review of the Costs and Impacts of Integrating Variable Renewables into Power Grids.” *Nature Energy* 6(1), 72–83.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-00695-4)
  
  *A systematic review of what integrating variable renewables costs across the studies that have measured it.*


## 04. Storage and flexibility

**Required**

- **Berg (2026).** “Energy System Models.” Read section 4.  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/energy-system-models.pdf)
  
  *A battery in the dispatch model: the arbitrage band, what arbitrage does to prices, ramping constraints, and what storage does to the value of wind.*
- **Zerrahn, Schill and Kemfert (2018).** “On the Economics of Electrical Storage for Variable Renewable Energy Sources.” *European Economic Review* 108, 259–279.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.euroecorev.2018.07.004) · [Open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.07885)
  
  *The first workshop paper. How much storage a renewable system actually needs, and why the answer is lower than usually assumed. Its small analytical model maps onto section 4 of the note.*
- **Ambec and Crampes (2021).** “Real-Time Electricity Pricing to Balance Green Energy Intermittency.” *Energy Economics* 94, 105074.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2020.105074) · [Open version](https://www.tse-fr.eu/sites/default/files/TSE/documents/doc/wp/2020/wp_tse_1087.pdf)
  
  *The second workshop paper. Flexible demand under real-time pricing as the alternative to storage, in a model small enough to solve by hand.*

**Supplementary**

- **Butters, Dorsey and Gowrisankaran (2025).** “Soaking up the Sun: Battery Investment, Renewable Energy, and Market Equilibrium.” *Econometrica* 93(3), 891–927.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA20411)
  
  *Battery investment in a market with a lot of solar, estimated structurally. Heavier than the two papers above; read it for what arbitrage revenue alone can and cannot pay for.*


## 05. Sector coupling and transmission

**Required**

- **Berg (2026).** “Energy System Models.” Read sections 5 and 6; 6.1 and 6.2 are background on grids and can be skimmed.  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/energy-system-models.pdf)
  
  *A heat market and a heat pump coupled to the power market, then bidding zones, corridors with losses, congestion rent, and who wins and loses from a cable.*
- **Ruhnau, Hirth and Praktiknjo (2020).** “Heating with Wind: Economics of Heat Pumps and Variable Renewables.” *Energy Economics* 92, 104967.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2020.104967) · [Open version](https://www.econstor.eu/handle/10419/219314)
  
  *The first workshop paper. Whether heat pumps help or hinder wind integration, and why the answer depends on the season. Section 5 of the note runs the same experiment.*
- **Gonzales, Ito and Reguant (2023).** “The Investment Effects of Market Integration: Evidence from Renewable Energy Expansion in Chile.” *Econometrica* 91(5), 1659–1693.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA20769) · [Open version](https://koichiroito.com/pdfs/Market_Integration_Gonzales_Ito_Reguant.pdf)
  
  *The second workshop paper. Chile joined two grids, and renewable investment responded. The investment effect is the one thing the fixed-capacity model of section 6 cannot produce, which is the bridge to the next lecture.*

**Supplementary**

- **Joskow and Tirole (2005).** “Merchant Transmission Investment.” *The Journal of Industrial Economics* 53(2), 233–264.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0022-1821.2005.00253.x)
  
  *Congestion rent as the return on a wire, and why a merchant investor builds too little of it.*
- **Hogan (2018).** “A Primer on Transmission Benefits and Cost Allocation.” *Economics of Energy & Environmental Policy* 7(1), 25–45.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.5547/2160-5890.7.1.whog)
  
  *Who benefits from a line and who should pay for it, in one primer. Behind section 6.7 of the note.*
- **Glaum, Neumann and Brown (2024).** “Offshore Power and Hydrogen Networks for Europe's North Sea.” *Applied Energy* 375, 123530.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2024.123530) · [Open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09721)
  
  *How much North Sea offshore wind you can integrate depends on what you may build to bring it ashore: 310 GW with today's point-to-point cables, 420 GW with meshed grids and offshore hydrogen. An infrastructure question, not a turbine question.*
- **Lüth, Seifert and Weibezahn (2023).** “How to Connect Energy Islands: Trade-Offs Between Hydrogen and Electricity Infrastructure.” *Applied Energy* 341, 121045.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2023.121045)
  
  *The Danish case, on the planned energy islands. Distance decides whether an island connects by cable or by hydrogen, and electrolyser investment turns out to track the hydrogen price far more than the carbon price.*


## 06. Investment

**Required**

- **Berg (2026).** “Energy System Models.” Read section 7, and appendix B for the annuity.  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/energy-system-models.pdf)
  
  *From dispatch to investment: annualised capital, screening curves, the greenfield problem, long-run zero profit, and what a rising carbon price builds.*
- **Brown, Neumann and Riepin (2025).** “Price Formation Without Fuel Costs: The Interaction of Demand Elasticity with Storage Bidding.” *Energy Economics* 146, 108483.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2025.108483)
  
  *The workshop paper. What sets the price when nobody has a fuel cost, and how little demand elasticity it takes to change the answer. The mechanism behind the demand blocks in section 7.*

**Supplementary**

- **Joskow (2011).** “Comparing the Costs of Intermittent and Dispatchable Electricity Generating Technologies.” *American Economic Review: Papers & Proceedings* 101(3), 238–241.
  
  *Four pages on why comparing technologies by levelised cost is the wrong comparison.*
- **Borenstein (2012).** “The Private and Public Economics of Renewable Electricity Generation.” *Journal of Economic Perspectives* 26(1), 67–92.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.26.1.67)
  
  *A survey, written for economists, of what renewable generation is worth privately and socially.*


## 07. Expansion at European scale, and the limits of the model

**Required**

- **Berg (2026).** “Energy System Models.” Read sections 8 and 9, and appendix E.  
  [Link](https://github.com/ChampionApe/EnergyEconomics/blob/main/notes/energy-system-models.pdf)
  
  *The model at continental scale under a carbon budget, the division of labour between storage technologies, hydrogen; then what changes with the weather year, the cost catalogue and foresight, and what the model cannot say.*
- **Victoria et al. (2019).** “The Role of Storage Technologies Throughout the Decarbonisation of the Sector-Coupled European Energy System.” *Energy Conversion and Management* 201, 111977.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enconman.2019.111977) · [Open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.06936)
  
  *The workshop paper, and the one section 8 of the note is written against: batteries for the daily solar cycle, hydrogen for wind's longer swings, and neither of them until emissions are cut past about 80%. Appendix E tests two of its claims directly.*

**Supplementary**

- **Neumann, Zeyen and Victoria (2023).** “The Potential Role of a Hydrogen Network in Europe.” *Joule* 7(8), 1793–1817.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2023.06.016) · [Open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05816)
  
  *Prices a European hydrogen network at up to 26 bn EUR a year, most of it repurposed gas pipeline. It is also the single largest thing our own model leaves out.*
- **Chyong, Pollitt and Reiner (2024).** “Modelling Flexibility Requirements in Deep Decarbonisation Scenarios: The Role of Conventional Flexibility and Sector Coupling Options in the European 2050 Energy System.” *Energy Strategy Reviews* 52, 101322.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esr.2024.101322)
  
  *A taxonomy rather than a headline number: it names the full menu of what "flexibility" means in 2050 and who supplies each part, including transmission as a flexibility source in its own right.*
- **Odenweller et al. (2026).** “REMIND-PyPSA-Eur: Integrating Power System Flexibility into Sector-Coupled Energy Transition Pathways.” *Progress in Energy* 8, 025001.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2510.04388) · [Open version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04388)
  
  *Couples a long-horizon climate-economy model to an hourly power model, and finds a striking asymmetry: flexible loads pay below-average electricity prices while heat pumps pay almost double, because their demand peaks when the system is tight.*
- **Bushnell and Smith (2025).** “Modeling Uncertainty in Climate Policy: An Application to the US Inflation Reduction Act.” *Environmental and Energy Policy and the Economy* 6, 4–41.  
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/733355)
  
  *How to model policy uncertainty in a climate policy analysis, on the US Inflation Reduction Act. Behind section 9 of the note.*
